title: Navy band at Great Lakes and the New Orleans beat
summary: He joined the Navy band in 1942 and taught Northern drummers parade-style bass drum; he describes George Williams and the band.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: I remember one time, excuse me for interrupting, you were telling us how, I think it was up when you were playing at the Paddock or at the Mardi Gras, one of those two places one night. You were talking quite a while about when you played at the Navy band, you went up there and they recognized immediately that you had a different kind of a beat.

I did, yeah. I did, yeah. Well, I was, when the band used to drill out on the fields, we had lots of drummers up there from the north, didn't understand the parade music. And I made all together two bass drums, two drummers, with good orchestra drummers. And I learned them how to play the bass drum in parade style. They already know the music for dance band, but they didn't understand the New Orleans style. And our band, the place of taking the 8th week training up there, we stood up there 3 months and 21 days. Because our chief was still down here, the custom house, Chief Cooper. And we had to stay up there and just, after our boot training was over in 8 weeks, we'd just lay around there and play all the graduation exercises and all the inspections on Saturdays.

Can you pin down and tell us what is the difference between the New Orleans beat and the other, can you explain any of that? Well I wouldn't know that. I didn't know that. Can you explain any of that?

Yes, it's a single beat you had, a steady single beat you had on a bass drum, you know, playing these different styles of marches. But they raid our whole band in New Orleans, in Great Lakes, when we was formerly, a band consisted of 23 men and one with the chief make 24. When we break it down to 15 or 16-piece dance obviously, we didn't have no special arrangement during the training time, so we played stock music in the training camp. And they considered it mostly like New Orleans style with the attack. Other members of the naval, I mean musicians of the naval barracks, they considered it as New Orleans style. That's the way they did it, they considered it, you understand? And then when we played, one day I was told, doing a graduation exercise when it was all over, I was greeted by some of the sailors with the nice tempo I had on the bass drum. I was playing bass drum at that time with the Navy band. And they agreed on the tempo I had. And that's why, from that day on, I was asked by two other good top drummers about how to make them attacks, you understand? But learning, because they were puzzling, come down to playing that two-fold and six-eighth music, which I still said it was good to orchestra drum, but that had them kind of puzzled. Well, we already had it through playing the funeral bands and prayers and around, we already knew that, you know, commit that to memories. You didn't worry about the music too much, but you can feel it. You can almost feel them marches, you know, through playing, especially the drummer. And that's why I said it in our instrument. We had another fellow who died recently by the name of Booker, Washington, we always would call him Booker, bass player. He learned lots of fellows up there how to play the bass on too for parade bands and different marching bands like that, Booker. And he, when we got down to Al Jays, he's a fellow by the name of playing some of these rock and roll artists called Frank Field. He learned him how to play the bass. Yeah, he's Frank Field. He used to come down here with George Williams, piano player, which was the leader of the Navy band, assistant leader you could say, piano player. Well, he's played all of this in the piano, George Williams, trumpet, saxophone and piano. And he arranged, put in this, Claiborne Williams' oldest son.
I was going to say he was Claiborne, I was going to ask if he was...

Claiborne Williams, from Napoleonville, Louisiana. Claiborne Williams' oldest son. That's George Williams. Well, he arranged and he made first class rake in the Navy band. And he did all the arrangements for the Navy band. Him and a fellow by the name of Boyt Traynor Adams from Tyler, Texas. There's two arrangements. But George was in charge of the band, George Williams.
Harold Dejean was in one of those bands.

Harold Dejean was in our same unit. Harold Dejean. Gilbert Jung, Henry Russ. That's all the fellas from this. That's the two men that we all joined together, was Henry Russ and Gilbert Jung. We all joined the Navy, the Navy band the same day. And from that time on, well, we just got out of the Navy. I'm trying to think now. I came back in the field and played several... did some funeral work with Peter Bocca and them. I think at that time it was called the brass band. It was considered the onward, part of the onward brass band. I might have the name wrong, but I think...
Right after the war, yeah, after I got out of the Navy.
When did you get out of the Navy?
